title: What a ZIA firewall log record is: aggregates, action and field names
aliases: firewall log vs web log field names

prose.text: A firewall log record describes a firewall session, and one record can stand for several aggregated sessions. Field names also differ from the web log for the same data.

action-values.statement: The Firewall Insights Logs Action filter, for firewall and IPS policy actions, includes the traffic that might be blocked due to a web policy violation after passing through the firewall module; its values include Allow due to insufficient app data, Block/Drop, Block/ICMP, Block/Reset, IPS Drop, IPS Reset, Dropped due to internal error, Bypassed due to missing config and Timed out while waiting for a config.

quotes: Action: Use this filter to limit the data to specific firewall and IPS policy actions.
This filter includes the traffic that might be blocked due to a web policy violation (as indicated in the Web Insights logs) after passing through the firewall module.
The transaction is logged as "Allow due to insufficient app data".
Block/Drop: Firewall policy rule is set to silently block packets that match the rule.
Block/ICMP: Policy rule was set to drop all packets that match the rule
Block/Reset: Firewall policy rule is set to Block/Reset.
IPS Drop: IPS policy rule is set to silently block packets that match the rule.
IPS Reset: IPS policy rule is set to Block/Reset.
Dropped due to internal error: This action is logged when the Firewall has received the user-side traffic but it fails to establish the internet-side connection
Bypassed due to missing config: This action is logged when
Timed out while waiting for a config: This action is logged when

internal-error.statement: Dropped due to internal error is logged when the firewall received the user-side traffic but failed to establish the internet-side connection, so the flow was dropped; it might occur when the Service Edge infrastructure is momentarily overused.

quotes: Dropped due to internal error: This action is logged when the Firewall has received the user-side traffic but it fails to establish the internet-side connection
resulting in the traffic flow being dropped. This might occur when the Service Edge infrastructure is momentarily overused.

missing-config.statement: Bypassed due to missing config is logged when the Public Service Edge cannot establish a connection with the Zscaler Central Authority, so the flow passes through Zscaler Firewall or DNS without policy; it might occur when a specific user's or location's traffic arrives at the Service Edge for the first time. Timed out while waiting for a config is logged when the connection is established but the configuration does not arrive within the expected time, typically 5 seconds. The columns page says both might additionally appear under specific circumstances when Best Effort Policies or Fail Closed mode is used with partial configurations.

quotes: fails to establish a connection with the Zscaler Central Authority (CA), resulting in the traffic flow passing through Zscaler Firewall or DNS without policy application.
This might occur when traffic flow from a specific user or location arrives at the Service Edge for the first time and a connection to the CA is required to apply policies.
Timed out while waiting for a config: This action is logged when the Public Service Edge has established a connection with the CA
a connection to the CA is established but there is no response from the CA within the expected time frame.
the requested configuration does not arrive from the CA within the expected time period (typically 5 seconds).

If Best Effort Policies or Fail Closed mode is used when partial configurations are available on a Service Edge, the following policy actions might additionally appear under specific circumstances: Bypassed due to missing config and Timed out while waiting for config.

aggregate-totals.statement: The Firewall Insights Logs columns article describes, for aggregated sessions, the bytes sent from the server and the bytes received by the server as totals across all sessions in the aggregate, and the duration as the sum of the individual session durations; the Extranet columns article says the same.

quotes: For aggregated sessions, this is the total bytes sent from the server across all sessions in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this is the total bytes received by the server across all sessions in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this indicates the sum of individual session durations.
For aggregated sessions, this is the total bytes sent from the server across all sessions in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this is the total bytes received by the server across all sessions in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this indicates the sum of individual session durations.

rule-name-blocked-only.statement: The Firewall Insights Logs Rule Name column is displayed in the logs only when the traffic is blocked, and by default not for allowed traffic.

quotes: Rule Name: The name of the rule
This column is displayed in the logs only when the traffic is blocked. By default, this column is not displayed for allowed traffic.

bypass-traffic-rule.statement: The Zscaler Bypass Traffic rule appears in firewall logs when the web module does not accept control from the firewall module because the handshake ends abruptly during flow establishment, or when traffic comes from a firewall-enabled sublocation whose parent location or another sublocation under it is not firewall-enabled, owing to latency in identifying the location differences, as in X-Forwarded-For setups.

quotes: The web module does not accept the control for the traffic evaluation from the firewall module because the handshake abruptly terminates during flow establishment.
The traffic is forwarded from a firewall-enabled sublocation but not enabled for the parent location or another sublocation under the same parent location.
This happens due to the latency in identifying these location differences, such as in the X-Forwarded-For (XFF) configuration.

icmp-ports.statement: For ICMP the Firewall Insights Logs source port shows the ICMP Identifier and the destination port shows as the ICMP Sequence Number.

quotes: This means, for ICMP, the source port shows the ICMP Identifier.
This means, for ICMP, the destination port shows as ICMP Sequence Number.

user-blank.statement: A blank User in Firewall Insights Logs means location-based authentication is set.

quotes: User: The user name. If this is blank, then location-based authentication is set.

sipa-server-ip.statement: With Source IP Anchoring for a URL or domain, the Firewall Insights Logs show the IP address 0.0.0.1 for the server to indicate the internal redirection, because the client request is forwarded to Private Access and the server IP is not logged at the proxy layer.

quotes: When you use Source IP Anchoring for the URL or domain, Zscaler doesn't log the server IP address at the proxy layer because the client request is forwarded to Private Access (ZPA), and the proxy code is already completed.
Therefore, the IP address 0.0.0.1 is logged to indicate the internal redirection within Zscaler.

severity-buckets.statement: The Firewall Insights Logs threat severity values follow the threat score: Critical for 90–100, High for 75–89, Medium for 46–74, Low for 1–45 and None for 0.

quotes: Critical: If the value of the threat score is 90–100.
High: If the value of the threat score is 75–89.
Medium: If the value of the threat score is 46–74.
Low: If the value of the threat score is 1–45.
None: If the value of the threat score is 0.

advanced-firewall-fqdns.statement: Client Destination Name and DNAT Destination Name are FQDN columns for Advanced Firewall, each holding the last session's value on an aggregate.

quotes: Client Destination Name: The client destination FQDN for Advanced Firewall. For aggregated sessions, this is the client destination FQDN of the last session in the aggregate.
DNAT Destination Name: The DNAT FQDN for Advanced Firewall. For aggregated sessions, this is the DNAT FQDN of the last session in the aggregate.

firewall-log-type.statement: A TCP Firewall feed's Firewall Log Type offers Full Session Logs, Aggregate Logs, or both, Full Session Logs being the option that log each session that matches the rule individually except web (HTTP/HTTPS) and FTP/FTPS sessions that match the same Allow rule over a time window, and Aggregate Logs, which group sessions by user, rule, network service and network application and record them periodically within an approximately 15-minute window. Full session logs do not include sessions recorded as part of aggregated entries, and the excluded web and FTP sessions are always available as aggregated entries, with detailed transactions in Web logs.

quotes: Both Session and Aggregate Logs
Full Session Logs: Logs each session that matches the rule individually, except for web (HTTP/HTTPS) and FTP/FTPS sessions that match the same Allow rule over a time window.
Full session logs do not include sessions that are recorded as part of aggregated entries.
Aggregate Logs: Groups individual sessions based on {user, rule, network service, network application}, and records them periodically within an approximately 15-minute time window.
These sessions are always available as aggregated entries in Firewall logs (with detailed web and FTP transactions in Web logs).

firewall-log-type-http-cloud.statement: The HTTP Firewall and Cloud Firewall feed articles offer the same Firewall Log Type options as the TCP Firewall article: Full Session Logs (each matching session individually, except web (HTTP/HTTPS) and FTP/FTPS sessions that match the same Allow rule over a time window, which Firewall logs always record as aggregated entries), Aggregate Logs (sessions grouped on {user, rule, network service, network application} and recorded periodically within an approximately 15-minute time window), or Both Session and Aggregate Logs, which includes all log data from both.

quotes: Full Session Logs: Logs each session that matches the rule individually, except for web (HTTP/HTTPS) and FTP/FTPS sessions that match the same Allow rule over a time window.
Aggregate Logs: Groups individual sessions based on {user, rule, network service, network application}, and records them periodically within an approximately 15-minute time window.
Both Session and Aggregate Logs
Full Session Logs: Logs each session that matches the rule individually, except for web (HTTP/HTTPS) and FTP/FTPS sessions that match the same Allow rule over a time window.
Firewall logs always record those web and FTP sessions as aggregated entries.
Aggregate Logs: Groups individual sessions based on {user, rule, network service, network application}, and records them periodically within an approximately 15-minute time window.
Both Session and Aggregate Logs: Includes all log data captured in full session logs and aggregated logs.
Full Session Logs: Logs each session that matches the rule individually, except for web (HTTP/HTTPS) and FTP/FTPS sessions that match the same Allow rule over a time window.
Firewall logs always record those web and FTP sessions as aggregated entries.
Aggregate Logs: Groups individual sessions based on {user, rule, network service, network application}, and records them periodically within an approximately 15-minute time window.
Both Session and Aggregate Logs: Includes all log data captured in full session logs and aggregated logs.

agg-flag.statement: The aggregate field indicates whether the Firewall session is aggregated, and numsessions is the number of sessions that were aggregated.

quotes: | %s{aggregate} | Indicates whether the Firewall session is aggregated
| %d{numsessions} | The number of sessions that were aggregated

last-session.statement: On an aggregated session, csip, csport, cdip, cdport, tsip, sdport, sdip, ssip and ssport each hold the value of the last session in the aggregate.

quotes: For aggregated sessions, this is the client source IP address of the last session in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this is the client source port of the last session in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this is the client destination IP address of the last session in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this is the client destination port of the last session in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this is the client's tunnel IP address corresponding to the last session in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this is the server destination port of the last session in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this is the server destination IP address of the last session in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this is the server source IP address of the last session in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this is the server source port of the last session in the aggregate.

undercount.statement: An aggregated record carries one set of addresses and ports for several sessions, so counting distinct addresses from aggregate records undercounts the addresses seen.
undercount.conditions: Follows from last-session values on a record that stands for numsessions sessions.

avgduration.statement: avgduration is the average session duration in milliseconds, if the sessions were aggregated.

quotes: The average session duration, in milliseconds, if the sessions were aggregated

srcip-country-agg.statement: srcip_country is determined by the client IP address location, and logs carry no source country for aggregated sessions that are allowed.

quotes: | %s{srcip_country} | The traffic's source country, which is determined by the client IP address location.
There is no source country value in logs for aggregated sessions that are allowed.

action-two-values.statement: The firewall action field is described as the action the service took on the transaction: Allowed or Blocked.

quotes: | %s{action} | The action that the service took on the transaction: Allowed or Blocked

rulelabel-unqualified.statement: The firewall rulelabel is described as the rule applied to the transaction with no Block-only qualifier, unlike the web log rulelabel, which applies only to Block rules; its example is the Default Firewall Filtering Rule.

quotes: | %s{rulelabel} | The name of the rule that was applied to the transaction | Default Firewall Filtering Rule | Rule Name
| %s{rulelabel} | The name of the rule that was applied to the transaction. Applies only to Block rules, not Allow. | URL_Filtering_1, URL_Filtering_2 | Blocked Policy Name

severity-typo.statement: The firewall field is threat_severity, and its description names that same field; severity relates directly to threat_score, so a score from 90 to 100 gives Critical.
severity-typo.conditions: Corrected on recapture (2026-10-18): previously "The firewall field is threat_severity, but its description refers to the web log name threatseverity; severity relates directly to threat_score, so a score from 90 to 100 gives Critical.".

quotes: | %s{threat_severity} | The severity of the threat detected in the Firewall session by the IPS engine. The severity relates directly to the threat score. For example, if the value of %d{threat_score} is between 90 and 100, then the value of %s{threat_severity} is Critical.

threat-score-source.statement: threat_score runs from 0 to 100, from the least to the greatest threat, and ThreatLabz assigns the score to the threat in the Zscaler Threat Library.

quotes: The score is assigned to the threat by Zscaler ThreatLabz and reflected in the Zscaler Threat Library.
The score ranges from 0–100, from the least to the greatest threat.

flags-1-0.statement: ips_custom_signature and bypassed_session are numeric flags with values 1 or 0; 1 means a custom IPS signature rule was applied, or that traffic bypassed Zscaler Client Connector.

quotes: | %d{ips_custom_signature} | Indicates if a custom IPS signature rule was applied. It is a numeric value (1 or 0). | 1 indicates a custom IPS rule 0 indicates a non-custom IPS rule |

| %d{bypassed_session} | Indicates whether the traffic bypassed the Zscaler Client Connector. It is a numeric value (1 or 0). | 1 indicates that the traffic bypassed Zscaler Client Connector 0 indicates that the traffic did not bypass Zscaler Client Connector |

country-forms.statement: srcip_country holds a country name such as United States, while destcountry holds an abbreviated code such as USA.

quotes: | %s{srcip_country} | The traffic's source country, which is determined by the client IP address location.
for aggregated sessions that are allowed. | United States | Source Country |
| %s{destcountry} | The abbreviated code of the country of the destination IP address | USA | Dest Country |

country-forms-not-comparable.statement: Because srcip_country carries a country name and destcountry an abbreviated code, the two fields are not directly comparable without mapping one form to the other.
country-forms-not-comparable.conditions: Follows from the documented example values; the source does not discuss comparing the two fields.

bytes-direction.statement: inbytes counts bytes sent from the server to the client and outbytes bytes sent from the client to the server.

quotes: | %ld{inbytes} | The number of bytes sent from the server to the client
| %ld{outbytes} | The number of bytes sent from the client to the server

nw-fields.statement: nwapp is described as the network application that was accessed and nwsvc as the network service that was used.

quotes: | %s{nwapp} | The network application that was accessed
| %s{nwsvc} | The network service that was used

aggregation-rule.statement: With the Standard Firewall subscription allowed sessions are logged in aggregate form and every blocked session gets its own detailed log; detailed logging of all sessions needs Advanced Firewall, while DNS transactions get detailed logs with both. Aggregation is done within a 15-minute window over User, Rule Slot, Network Service, Network Application and IP Category: consecutive sessions with the same values in these fields produce a single log whose remaining fields are taken from the last session in the window.

quotes: For the Standard Firewall subscription, allowed sessions are logged in aggregate form, resulting in fewer logs for the allowed transactions. Blocked transactions have detailed logs and produce a log for every blocked session.
If you want detailed logging for all sessions, including blocked and allowed transactions, you must have Advanced Firewall.
However, detailed logging for DNS transactions is available with both Standard and Advanced Firewall.
Logs are aggregated for each of the following fields within a 15-minute time window: User, Rule Slot, Network Service, Network Application, and IP Category.
For consecutive sessions with the same values across these fields, Zscaler only records a single log, in which the remaining fields are taken from the last session in the 15-minute time window.

aggregate-counters-source.summary: The Firewall Insights Logs columns article describes aggregated byte counters as totals across all sessions in the aggregate and the duration as the sum of session durations, while the NSS firewall output format says an aggregated log's remaining fields are taken from the last session in the 15-minute window; the HTTP Firewall feed article's byte filters agree with the totals, and its Durations filter gives the average.

quotes: For aggregated sessions, this is the total bytes sent from the server across all sessions in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this indicates the sum of individual session durations.

positions.says: For aggregated sessions the bytes sent from the server are a total across all sessions in the aggregate and the duration is the sum of the individual session durations.

quotes: For consecutive sessions with the same values across these fields, Zscaler only records a single log, in which the remaining fields are taken from the last session in the 15-minute time window.
| %ld{inbytes} | The number of bytes sent from the server to the client | 10,000 | Inbound Bytes |

positions.says: A single log records the remaining fields from the last session in the 15-minute window, and inbytes is described as the number of bytes sent from the server to the client, with no aggregate wording.

quotes: For aggregated sessions, this is the total bytes sent from the server across all sessions in the aggregate.
For aggregated sessions, this indicates the average session duration.

positions.says: The HTTP Firewall feed article's byte filters say the value for aggregated sessions is the total bytes across all sessions in the aggregate, agreeing with the Insights Logs columns, while its Durations filter says it indicates the average session duration, against the Insights sum.

aggregate-counters-source.impact: Summing inbytes, outbytes and durationms over aggregate records gives different results if they hold the last session's values rather than totals; the HTTP Firewall feed article gives byte totals and an average Duration for aggregated sessions, and no page says which of these a feed's own inbytes, outbytes and duration fields hold.

aggregation-keys.summary: The HTTP and Cloud Firewall feed articles group aggregate logs on four keys, while the NSS firewall output format lists five aggregation fields; IP Category is clearly absent from the feed articles' list, and their "rule" may or may not be the output format's Rule Slot.

quotes: Aggregate Logs: Groups individual sessions based on {user, rule, network service, network application}, and records them periodically within an approximately 15-minute time window.

positions.says: Aggregate Logs group individual sessions on user, rule, network service and network application, recorded within an approximately 15-minute time window.

quotes: Aggregate Logs: Groups individual sessions based on {user, rule, network service, network application}, and records them periodically within an approximately 15-minute time window.

positions.says: The Cloud Firewall feed article gives the same four keys.

quotes: Logs are aggregated for each of the following fields within a 15-minute time window: User, Rule Slot, Network Service, Network Application, and IP Category.

positions.says: Logs are aggregated for User, Rule Slot, Network Service, Network Application and IP Category within a 15-minute time window.

aggregation-keys.impact: Whether sessions that differ only in IP Category aggregate into one record depends on which page is read; the pages do not say whether the feed articles' shorter list is complete (the TCP article's matching sentence is in firewall-log-type).

action-value-set.summary: The NSS firewall output format describes the action field as Allowed or Blocked, while the Firewall Insights Logs Action filter lists firewall and IPS policy actions beyond those two.

quotes: | %s{action} | The action that the service took on the transaction: Allowed or Blocked | Blocked | Action |

positions.says: The action is Allowed or Blocked.

quotes: Action: Use this filter to limit the data to specific firewall and IPS policy actions.
Block/Drop: Firewall policy rule is set to silently block packets that match the rule.
IPS Drop: IPS policy rule is set to silently block packets that match the rule.

positions.says: The Action filter lists specific firewall and IPS policy actions, among them Block/Drop and IPS Drop.

action-value-set.impact: A query that matches the action field against Allowed and Blocked misses the console's other values if a feed carries them; the pages do not say whether the console values are what the feed's action field holds.

rulelabel-display.title: Whether allowed firewall transactions carry a rule name in the feed
rulelabel-display.detail: The Firewall Insights Logs Rule Name column is displayed only when the traffic is blocked (rule-name-blocked-only). The NSS firewall output format describes rulelabel as the name of the rule applied to the transaction and says nothing about display, so no source shows whether the feed's rulelabel is empty for allowed traffic or the restriction is a console display rule.

aggregate-counters.title: How byte and duration counters behave on an aggregated record
aggregate-counters.detail: Unverified legacy statement: the CSV does not say what triggers aggregation (idle timeout, volume, rule) or whether it is configurable, nor how inbytes, outbytes, durationms and avgduration behave on aggregates (sum, maximum or last session), since they carry no last-session wording. The trigger is now sourced (aggregation-rule: Standard Firewall subscription, allowed sessions, a 15-minute window over five fields). Still open: whether inbytes, outbytes and durationms count only the last session, as 'the remaining fields are taken from the last session' would suggest, or the whole aggregate, given that numsessions and avgduration are aggregate values. A burst of identical allowed sessions from one source on a Standard Firewall tenant would show it. The Firewall Insights Logs columns article describes the byte counters as totals across the aggregate and the duration as the sum of the sessions (aggregate-totals), against the NSS last-session wording; see the divergence aggregate-counters-source.
aggregate-counters.blocks: Summing bytes or counting sessions from aggregated records.

srcip-country-aggregate.title: Why aggregated allowed sessions have no source country
srcip-country-aggregate.detail: Unverified legacy statement: the CSV states that aggregated allowed sessions carry no srcip_country but does not say why; the legacy reading is that the lookup happens at block time only, which is not confirmed. A mixed allowed and blocked aggregate test would show it.
srcip-country-aggregate.blocks: Geographic reporting on allowed firewall traffic.

action-precedence.title: Which subsystem fills action when firewall, IPS and DNAT disagree
action-precedence.detail: Unverified legacy statement: the CSV does not say what action shows when the firewall allows and IPS blocks, whether dnat is Yes on a firewall block, what an IPS detect-only hit shows, or whether action is the first or final outcome. Triggering each combination and reading action with threatcat, dnat and rulelabel would show it.

nwapp-vs-nwsvc.title: How nwapp and nwsvc relate
nwapp-vs-nwsvc.detail: Unverified legacy statement: whether nwapp is a DPI application and nwsvc a port-derived service, or the reverse, whether both are always filled, and what they hold for non-IP traffic such as ICMP is not stated. Sending HTTP on a nonstandard port and a tunnel would show it.
nwapp-vs-nwsvc.blocks: Choosing which field names the application the user accessed.
